source.title: Implicit bias produces neural scaling laws in learning curves, from perceptrons to deep networks
source.authors: Francesco D'Amico; Dario Bocchi; M. Negri

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. The paper is not the original source for the claim.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own image-classification and perceptron results that refine the scope of scaling laws: learning curves have distinct regimes, and fitted exponents and predictive agreement vary with dataset, optimizer, regularization, and norm. It does not test language-model cross-entropy or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The study measures generalization/test error, primarily in image classification, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy. It varies training-set size and a norm-based measure during training, but holds architecture sizes fixed. It does not report a parameter-count or compute-budget sweep. Rows below cover its own power-law and curve-collapse results; cited language-model scaling results are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of minimum image-classification test error against training-set size P for CNN, ResNet and ViT on MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 (γmeas, Table 1). That is a data-scaling result in a non-text setting, which bears on V5. Exponents differ across datasets and architectures, and the study also varies weight decay and optimizer, which bears on V7. Its main contribution, error versus a norm during training, is a different construct. It does not vary parameters or compute and does not study language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. The authors find two norm-based dynamical scaling laws across CNN, ResNet and ViT on MNIST and CIFAR, and their product recovers the end-of-training error-versus-data exponent under the spectral-complexity norm. Weight decay and SGD change the dynamical exponents γ1 and γ2 but not the end exponent. Alternative norms reproduce the qualitative picture but give incompatible γpred. The record's phrase that exponents depend on regularization and optimizer should apply only to the dynamical exponents.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes image-classification generalization error and perceptron logistic-loss learning curves against training-set size and norm-based complexity. It does not use the original language-model cross-entropy versus parameter/data/compute scaling procedure or test compute-optimal model/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported exponents vary with dataset, optimizer, weight decay, norm definition, and loss. The paper reports an early regime and a distinct late regime; the learning curves are plotted against norm rather than epoch count.

fits_no_version.finding: Test error, plotted against a spectral-complexity norm during training, follows a P-independent early power law. Curves collapse after rescaling by the minimum point.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning curves indexed by weight norm show a universal early power law and data-dependent collapse (dynamical norm scaling).

fits_no_version.finding: The norm at minimum test error grows as a power of P; multiplying the two exponents reproduces the data-scaling exponent only for the spectral-complexity norm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The end-of-training data exponent factorises as γ1·γ2 of the norm-based laws.

fits_no_version.finding: Analytic fixed-norm perceptron: optimal error scales as α^−1/2, matching Bayes-optimal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher–student perceptron learning curves follow analytic power laws in data ratio.

record.problems: The authors limit deep-network experiments to image classification and a few fixed-size standard architectures; they do not vary parameter count or study language models. Results depend on the chosen norm, and alternative norms give predicted exponents incompatible with measured ones. Some model runs had only 5 repetitions, while smaller models reached 30; the authors report larger errors and reduced statistics for weight-decay ResNets. The perceptron-to-deep-network comparison is described as mainly qualitative.
record.rows_left_out: The paper includes plotted learning-curve trajectories and curve-collapse figures (Figures 1–4 and 6–21); individual plotted coordinates are not extracted because values are not tabulated. Tables 1–5 and explicit text statements record the quantitative exponent results and reported comparisons. No result-bearing item was otherwise omitted within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small to much larger runs. The authors only suggest the shape of the curve could transfer across dataset sizes.
Fixed-compute allocation of parameters and tokens.

Only error versus data size for image classifiers is tested. Untested: scaling with model size or compute, generative image/video loss, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. The CIFAR P range (6000–46000, or 4000–48000) is under one order of magnitude; MNIST spans about 2.7 orders.
Untested: parameter counting, schedule length, fitting method, and effects on a compute-optimal split.

missing.what: γmeas for the same no-weight-decay setting differs between Table 1 and Table 5. CNN CIFAR10 is 0.25 vs 0.181, the latter on a different P grid. ResNet is 0.56 vs 0.500 and ViT 0.21 vs 0.175. This shows the fitted exponent's sensitivity to P grid or run set.
P ranges per dataset that the γmeas fits span: MNIST 89–48000; CIFAR 4000/6000–46000/48000.

record.verdict_notes: Classification error at the best training epoch, not cross-entropy loss. Architectures are fixed-size, so no parameter scaling is tested. Weight-decay and SGD rows are linked to V7 only: their γmeas shows no optimizer or regularization dependence. The power law persisting under those choices is also consistent with V5. The γ2 values for ViT (18–21) are suspicious as exponents, but those rows are linked to no version. The 0.25 vs 0.181 γmeas discrepancy for CNN CIFAR10 is not explained by the authors.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.

No test of extrapolating language-model loss from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger. The paper discusses predicting curve shape across dataset sizes but does not run the stated language-model extrapolation test.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep between model parameters and training tokens; its λopt versus training-set-size result is not a compute-optimal model/data allocation.
Architectures are compared, but not at matched parameter count in a controlled depth/width sweep.
The paper tests image-classification test error and a perceptron setting, not image/video generative-model loss, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, transfer, or language-model pretraining.
No downstream-task performance versus language-model pretraining loss or language-model scale is measured.

The study tests dependence on dataset, optimizer, weight decay, norm definition, and loss in its settings. It does not test parameter-counting choices, language-model training schedules, or how fitting choices alter a compute-optimal parameter/token split.

rows.subject: perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Analyze fixed-norm teacher–student perceptrons trained with logistic loss; plot generalization error against loss parameter λ.
rows.measure: Early-regime generalization-error power-law exponent versus λ.
rows.value: For the fixed-norm perceptron, γ1 = −1/2 in the text's exponent convention for ε̂gen ∝ λ−γ1; the analytic derivation gives ε ∼ (αλ)−1/2 for 1 ≪ λ ≪ α.
rows.note: The text reports a power-law regime and states its validity range.
rows.check: Analytic teacher–student perceptron error versus loss sharpness or norm; a toy construct outside the versions. The record's sign convention is also confused: the exponent magnitude is 1/2.

rows.subject: perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Fit the optimal loss parameter as a function of data ratio in the fixed-norm teacher–student analysis.
rows.measure: Scaling exponent for λopt versus α.
rows.note: The fixed-norm result is described as a power law.
rows.check: λopt versus α in the perceptron; not a loss scaling measure.

rows.subject: perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Fit the optimal relative generalization error as a function of data ratio in the fixed-norm teacher–student analysis.
rows.measure: Scaling exponent for optimal relative generalization error versus α.
rows.note: The result is described as matching the Bayes-optimal predictor's generalization error.
rows.check: Analytic perceptron error ∝ α^−1/2. This is a classical statistical-mechanics result, not a modality or training regime named by V5.

rows.subject: perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Numerically fit the free-norm perceptron training curves and their optimal norm versus data ratio.
rows.measure: Fitted dynamical exponents γ1 for error versus norm and γ2 for optimal norm versus α.
rows.baseline: Fixed-norm analytic exponents are reported as γ1 = 0.5 and γ2 = 1.0.
rows.note: The authors say the free-norm fits are not compatible with the fixed-norm results considering errors, though the differences are only of the order of 5%.
rows.check: Free-norm perceptron dynamical exponents.

rows.subject: perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Compare training curves using mean squared error rather than cross-entropy.
rows.measure: Presence of early error-versus-norm power law and dependence of λopt on α.
rows.baseline: Cross-entropy perceptron analysis in the main text.
rows.value: The text states no early-training power law of the tested form is observed and λopt is constant, not following the second scaling law.
rows.note: This is an explicit loss-choice counterexample to the perceptron learning-curve scaling phenomenology.
rows.check: MSE perceptron counterexample concerns the study's dynamical laws, not loss scaling with resources.

relationships.condition: CNN, ResNet and ViT image classifiers on MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100; minimum test error versus training-set size
relationships.reason: Test error falls as a fitted power law in P for all nine architecture–dataset pairs (γmeas 0.12–0.69; R1–R9). The CIFAR fits span under one decade of P.
relationships.display_finding: Minimum test error fitted power laws in training-set size across all nine architecture–dataset pairs, with measured exponents of 0.12–0.69 and CIFAR ranges spanning less than one decade.

relationships.reason: Data-scaling exponents vary widely with dataset and architecture, e.g. CNN 0.55 on MNIST vs 0.16 on CIFAR100 (R1–R9).
relationships.display_finding: CNN data-scaling exponents are 0.55 on MNIST versus 0.16 on CIFAR100, illustrating variation across datasets and architectures.

relationships.condition: Optimizer (SGD vs Adam) and moderate weight decay, CIFAR
relationships.reason: The end-of-training data exponent stays compatible within error across these choices, per the authors (R28–R38). Only the study's dynamical exponents shift.
relationships.display_finding: End-of-training data exponents remained compatible within error across SGD, Adam and moderate weight decay, while dynamical exponents changed.
